opus-5.5.text:
I think the core reason is that we're entering a phase where high-quality data is becoming the real bottleneck. For a long time the scaling story was "add more compute, add more data," but the pool of good human-written tokens on the internet is finite. So if you can't easily get more data, the next best thing is to extract more intelligence out of every token you already have. That's what we call token efficiency, and the optimizer is one of the most fundamental levers for it.

Adam has been the default for almost a decade, and people kind of stopped questioning it. When we looked at Muon, the early results on small models were very promising. It seemed to learn noticeably more per token, roughly comparable to getting close to twice the effective data in some settings. That's a huge deal. If you think about it, a gain like that is equivalent to discovering a whole new internet's worth of data.

But the problem was that nobody had shown it actually works at frontier scale. Lots of ideas look good on small models and then fall apart when you go to hundreds of billions or a trillion parameters. So we had to do real engineering work. For example, we found you need proper weight decay, and you need to adjust the update scale so it behaves consistently with Adam across different parameter shapes. Otherwise things drift as training gets longer. Then when we scaled up further for K2, we hit training instability, the attention logits would blow up. That's why we developed what we call QK-Clip, which became MuonClip, to keep those logits in check without hurting performance. In the end we could train on trillions of tokens with basically no loss spikes, which honestly surprised even us.

So to me, it matters for two reasons. One is practical: it directly makes our models better given the same data and compute. The other is more philosophical. It shows that there's still a lot of room to innovate at the very bottom of the stack. Many people assume the foundations are settled and the only work left is at the application layer. I don't believe that. If you're willing to revisit first principles, like how you actually update the weights, you can still find big gains. And for a company like us, which doesn't have unlimited resources, that kind of efficiency is not optional, it's how we stay competitive.

r001.rationale: The response says small-model results looked promising and that attention logits blew up when scaling up for K2, but it does not say this instability is difficult to detect in small-scale experiments.

r002.rationale: It identifies QK-Clip, later called MuonClip, as a method developed to keep exploding attention logits in check during large-scale training.

r003.rationale: It says high-quality data is finite, so improving token efficiency—getting more intelligence from each token—motivates adapting the optimizer to improve models with the same data and compute.

fable-5.1.text:
Guest: I think it's important because, fundamentally, there's a lot of room left on the table in how we train these models. AdamW has been the default for years, and almost everything that's been built at scale is built on top of it. But AdamW was never designed for the kind of regime we're in now, where you're training hundreds of billions of parameters on trillions of tokens. It just happened to work well enough that nobody wanted to take the risk of changing it.

When we looked at Muon, the initial results on small models were very promising, roughly two times better token efficiency compared to AdamW. That's a huge number. If that holds up at scale, it means you can get the same model with half the compute, or a much better model with the same compute. For a company like ours, where compute is always the bottleneck, that kind of gain changes what's possible.

But the key question was whether it would actually transfer. A lot of optimizer papers show nice curves at a few hundred million parameters and then the gains disappear when you scale up. So the real work was figuring out what breaks. Two things stood out: the weight updates tended to grow in a way that caused instability, and the update magnitudes were inconsistent across layers of different shapes. We added weight decay and adjusted the per-parameter update scale, and with those changes it stayed stable and kept its advantage at much larger sizes. That's what let us train Moonlight, and it's also why we had the confidence to use it for Kimi K2 at a trillion parameters.

The broader reason I care about this is that pretraining efficiency compounds. Every improvement in the optimizer feeds into every model you train afterward. Architecture changes, data changes, those matter too, but the optimizer is one of the few things that sits underneath everything. If we can move the field from AdamW to something meaningfully better, that's a lasting contribution, not just a one-off model release.

r001.rationale: The response mentions instability at scale, but attributes it to growing weight updates. It does not identify maximum-logit instability or say that it is hard to detect in small-scale experiments.

r002.rationale: The response describes adding weight decay and adjusting update scale to address instability; it does not identify clipping as a mitigation for exploding maximum logits.

r003.rationale: The response cites better token efficiency as a motivation, but frames the constraint as compute being a bottleneck. It does not connect the motivation to a limited token budget.

astra-6.text:
I think the main reason is that, at very large scale, optimization efficiency has a huge impact on what we can achieve with a fixed compute budget. If we can reach the same model quality with fewer training steps, or get better quality with the same amount of compute, that’s a very valuable improvement.

Muon is interesting because it changes how we construct updates for weight matrices, using more of their matrix structure. But a promising optimizer at small scale doesn’t automatically become a practical optimizer for large language models. You have to make sure it remains stable, works efficiently in distributed training, and delivers gains after accounting for the cost of the optimizer itself.

So adapting Muon is important because it tests whether that optimization idea can translate into a real improvement in the economics of training large models.

sol-6.1.text:
Because at that scale, optimization efficiency has a very direct impact on what you can achieve with a fixed compute budget. If you can train more efficiently, you can either reach the same capability at lower cost or get a better model with the same resources.

Muon is interesting because it changes how we update weight matrices, which are central to language models. But an optimizer that looks promising at a smaller scale doesn’t automatically work well at a very large scale. You have to make sure it remains stable and that its benefits survive the realities of distributed training, memory constraints, and communication overhead.

So adapting Muon is about turning a promising optimization idea into something useful for large-scale training. The important question is whether it improves the quality you get per unit of compute.
